Death of Defenders

By: Latashia Naidoo | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What happens when those meant to uphold the law, become victims themselves? Carte Blanche investigates.

Unique Selling Point:
Lawyers are under threat in the Western Cape.
In recent years, attacks on members of the legal fraternity have become an occupational hazard - which often ends in death.

Summary:
There have been a string of hits and attempted hits on lawyers who have represent gangland figures especially of late, with fears that such a trend engenders could erode the integrity of the legal system.

Attacks on members of the legal fraternity are in the spotlight following the murder trial of Advocate Pete Mihalik, who represented Ralph Stanfield, the leader of the 28s gang, when Stanfield was charged with assault and intimidation.
He was killed outside a Cape Town private school in 2018.

The Cape Bar association says that violence against lawyers threatens to undermine criminal justice system.
Research conducted by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime in Cape Town and other investigators has revealed that some criminal lawyers get drawn into the gang ecosystem.
They can stray into the line of fire after disputes with clients.


Further information:
Two years after the assassination attempt on his life, Cape Town advocate Jakes van der Merwe is reminded of the incident everyday.
One of the two bullets that were fired at him is still lodged in his neck.
The high-profile criminal lawyer was shot by a masked man outside his home in Gardens in 2020.
His attacker remains at large.

In April of that same year, well-known Cape Town criminal lawyer William Booth survived what appeared to be an assassination attempt by two unknown males wearing face masks.
He was unhurt in the incident, but became yet another criminal lawyer to be targeted in shootings in Cape Town in recent years.
His perpetrators have not been arrested, either.

Script:


DEATH OF DEFENDERS: FINAL DRAFT
VO: A quiet street in Cape Town…
On a balmy summer morning…
A man stumbles out of his vehicle… clutching his neck…
VIZ: CCTV FOOTAGE
JAKES:
“I knew I got shot in my neck, and I know it was going to start bleeding now…And I knew, the faster I walk the more it would bleed, probably.
And I thought well now, ‘is this what it feels like to die?’”
VO: Civil attorney Jakes van der Merwe is lucky to be alive …
… after surviving a brazen assassination attempt outside his home in Gardens.
(SHOW MORE CCTV FOOTAGE)
VO:
CCTV footage of the attack on him shows a grey van pulling up next to Jakes’ Toyota Land Cruiser.
The driver fires two shots through the window – and speeds off.
The intended target – Jakes - is badly injured – but alive.
JAKES:
“The police just said to me that they can’t ensure my safety. And he said to me it was an organised attempt on my life, and that he’s 95% sure that the guy’s gonna come and finish the job.”
VO:
It’s two years later. The CCTV footage assisted the police in identifying Jakes’ would-be assassin - but said he fled the country within weeks after the attack.
VO:

Emails uncovered in the investigation showed the attacker’s grievances.
JAKES:
“This incident is an incident where the person has a huge grudge against lawyers, and he thinks that lawyers should be dealt with. And he started with me.”

LINK:
“Lawyers in the Western Cape are under siege - facing unprecedented attacks from criminal entities - hellbent on defeating the ends of justice. Now lawyers are asking: ‘who’s next?’”
VO:
Jakes is one of scores of lawyers in the province who’ve fallen victim to attacks, threats, and intimidation in recent years – simply for doing their jobs.
VO:
Since 2016, physical and online attacks have escalated…
VO:
…With at least four brutal murders of top legal minds in Cape Town alone.
VO:
Law associations say - an attack on lawyers is an attack on justice…
VIZ: CANDLE BEING BLOWN OUT

VO:

But some have already paid the ultimate price.
Mehraaj:
“Two or three guys came out with masks… and they came directly for Noorudien. And they shot him at close range.”
LINK:
“Six years ago, criminal lawyer Noorudien Hassan was shot and killed outside his house – execution style. His killers have never been arrested. His family believe that justice delayed is justice denied.”
VO:
Mehraaj Hassan never thought she would become a widow at 36…
VO:

Or that her 45-year-old husband - a criminal attorney working on high-profile gang-related cases - would meet such a violent end.
Claire: “It’s almost surreal; it sounds like a movie.”
Mehraaj:
“Well I often think, ‘why was he murdered? Was it such a big thing that you had to murder the man?”

VO:

Noorudien was father to two young children, a devoted husband, and pillar of his community.

VO:

At the same time, he represented some of Cape Town’s most notorious gang figureheads.
Claire: “Did he ever feel like his life was in danger?”
Mehraaj: “If he was getting threats or anything, he never said anything.”
VO:
Then in October 2018, Noorudien’s colleague and close friend, criminal advocate, Pete Mihalik, was also assassinated.
VO:

Like Noorudien, Pete had been known as a “gangster lawyer” who represented known high-fliers in Cape Town’s underworld.

VO:

Both their names were at the top of an alleged ‘hit list’.

VO:

And both their lives… snuffed out by the barrel of a hired gun.

(PAUSE)

VO:
Three men - Sizwe Biyela, Vuyile Maliti and Nkosinathi Khumalo - are currently on trial at the Western Cape High Court, charged with Mihalik’s murder…

VO:

Forensic analysis presented in court last week revealed that Biyela was the triggerman.

Noorudien Hassan’s killers… have never been found.

ESTABLISHING SHOTS OF SIMON

VO:

At the University of Cape Town, criminologist Dr Simon Howell tracks the interplay between the city’s underworld and mainstream society and business.

Claire:
“It seems like there’s a specific risk to criminal lawyers in the Western Cape. Why are we not seeing this trend as much in other provinces?”
SIMON:
“It’s primarily in the Western Cape that organised crime is so entrenched and has such deep roots into, you know, the legitimate sides of society as well.”
VIZ: TURF WARS, CRIME SCENES, COPS ON RAIDS, ETC (MOVING TO ABOVE)

VO: Cape Town’s glamorous exterior conceals an underbelly of organised crime…

…. an unending cycle of bloody reprisals has gripped these streets as gangs compete for protection money and drug turf in entertainment hotspots…

… to launder the proceeds of crime.

VO:

The courts have now become the battleground for rival kingpins… and the criminal lawyers fighting their legal battles: casualties on the frontlines.
SIMON:
“In many instances, lawyers will become involved in – maybe not directly, by association – will become involved in various criminal undertakings. Whether it be through payment structures, or whether it be through association with actual individuals – the result which actually is they endanger themselves.”
VO:

Every person accused of a crime is entitled to a defense…

… but with controversial clients the work of a criminal lawyer can become as fraught as it is lucrative…

… and in Cape Town, also deadly…

GRAPHIC: (With pictures and dates)

VO:

Noorudien Hassan was the first lawyer to be killed in a hit.

VO:

Pete Mihalik was executed outside his children’s Green Point school two years later.

VO:

In May 2019, criminal defence attorney David Mbazwana was shot and killed outside a spaza shop in Khayelitsha.

VO:

And in December that year, magistrate Vernon Jantjies died in a hail of bullets outside his linen shop in Lentegeur, Mitchells Plain.
VO:

Then in April 2020, prominent criminal lawyer William Booth survived an organised hit at his Cape Town home.

(PAUSE)

VO:

Many of these cases have now gone cold… (PAUSE) …

… those left behind, now anxious and uncertain.

LINK:
“The legal profession plays a pivotal role in the administration of justice. As officers of the court, lawyers need to be able to practice freely – without fear, favour or prejudice.”
CLAIRE:
“What do you understand about these people that carry out these attacks and these crimes? Are they just opportunistic individuals operating on their own?..”
Simon:
“Well it’s fundamentally, they are part of a larger criminal enterprise. And, I mean, the killings are carried out in the name of that enterprise…”
VO:

Legal bodies say these attacks represent a threat to the rule of law and democracy.

Clive Hendricks chairs the Cape Town Attorneys Association.

Clive:
“Some of those attacks that I’ve heard about doesn’t really make the news. But it starts small. And if it’s not dealt with appropriately, then those are the kind of things that escalates to what we’ve now seen in recent years.”

VO:

Clive says the profession needs protection… which the police alone can’t offer.

Clive:

“We’ve had conversations on our huge WhatsApp groups with thousands of lawyers that has raised complaints about certain challenges facing the legal profession.”

VO:
Lawyers across South Africa belong to the Whatsapp groups and share their worries over threats…

… but in the Western Cape, it’s the particular set of underworld factors that enhance the risk…


VO: The attacks have created a culture of paranoia…

People are scared.
Clive: “It is on the organised legal profession – speaking as a unified voice – to lead the charge for protection for… all stakeholders in the justice system.”
VO:

As the Cape Town law community continues to battle a faceless enemy – it’s left many considering ‘safer’ alternatives.

(PAUSE)
VO:
Yet despite coming so close to death, Jakes isn't prepared to give up his law career just yet.
JAKES:
“I know… I should either have been dead or I should have been paralysed. It’s not a miracle that I’m sitting here, it’s something – it’s a message for me in life.”
VO:
Meanwhile, Mehraaj doesn’t want her husband’s legacy reduced to a statistic…
… even after all this time, she still brings their children to spend time at his grave.
MEHRAAJ:
Claire: “So you say that they come and tell him and they catch him up on what’s happened in the last six years?”
M: “What’s happened, yes.”
C: “And does it bring comfort, do you think?”
M: “It does, it really does.”
END VIZ: C/U OF GRAVE SURROUNDED BY FLOWERS AND CARDS







PROMOS:

PROMO LINK 1:

Claire:
“In the world of criminal law, risks are ever present. But what happens when the law itself
Becomes a matter of life and death for its practitioners?”

PROMO LINK 2:
CLAIRE:
“Lawyers in the Western Cape are under siege.”

UPSOUND:
Clive:
“There is a concern – a concern over the safety of legal practitioners in general.”

VO:
But are these attacks an act of revenge or an attempt to silence?

JAKES: “This incident is an incident where the person has a huge grudge against lawyers, and he thinks that lawyers should be dealt with. And he started with me.”

PROMO LINK 3:

VO: It’s become an occupational hazard…

UPSOUND: Simon:
“If you want to stall or delay a case, one of the easiest ways is to remove or otherwise damage the individual who’s representing the accused.”

VO:
Lawyers in the Western Cape are under attack... and it sometimes leads to death…

Mehraaj:
“I often think, ‘why was he murdered? Was it such a big thing that you had to murder the man?”
